# The Curse of Granular Control


[Chelsey Sassine](https://medium.com/@chelseysassine?source=post_page---byline--ea1e5fb04c4e------------------------------------------)


5 min read


·


2 hours ago


--


*Why AI-era software needs process engineers*


Press enter or click to view image in full size


For a decade, one of my computer screens never changed. I traveled the world starting up refining and petrochemical units as a process engineer, and I always kept a dashboard open that showed the unit’s health at a glance.


Every assignment was a different unit, sometimes running a completely different technology, and the screen was almost always in a different language. It didn’t matter. I could still read it, and when something drifted, I knew before anyone called me.


Then I went to a coding bootcamp and became a software engineer. The first time I was on call, I did what I’d always done and opened the dashboard. It was in my own language, for code my own team had written. I still couldn’t read it. Nothing on it told me whether the code was behaving the way it was designed to. I didn’t bother opening it for my next shift.


That gap was the biggest difference I noticed after switching fields. Now that AI is writing more of our code, I think it’s about to become the most important one.


## The curse of granular control


When software engineers decide against comprehensive observability and robust testing, it’s often for the same reason. They write the code and trace the paths, so they “know” how it will behave. Watching it run in production is an afterthought when you feel like you already understand it.


This is the curse of granular control.


To be fair, software has built real operational discipline in SRE and the observability movement. But most of that work was split off into separate roles, away from the people designing the system. The person who wrote the code rarely watched it run.


## A software factory changes the deal


That arrangement held up as long as a human had read every line. AI is ending that. An AI-augmented system, or software factory, is starting to write and review the code.


In one sense, this is software growing up. Every mature engineering discipline eventually separated the people who design from the people who build. A civil engineer doesn’t pour the concrete for the bridge they designed. An electrical engineer doesn’t pull wire through the walls. That separation is what let those disciplines scale. Software now has its builder.


But when the factory writes the code, the feeling of understanding is gone, and nothing has replaced it to allow confident operation. Software engineers are expected to ship faster and own more surface area without producing slop or blowing a token budget. They’re giving up a craft they love without the support mature engineering disciplines rely on, like defined roles, proven tools, training paths, and shared norms for what “good” looks like.


That’s a lot. But I think chemical engineering can help.


## Chemical engineers never had granular control


While chemical engineers understand their processes deeply, they never get to watch them directly. The reactions are too complex to trace one by one, and you can’t see inside a reactor anyway. Like doctors, they reason about a system’s health from the outside, through interpreting signals from measurements they take.


They don’t get deterministic control either. The best they can do is make conditions favorable for the reactions they want and unfavorable for the ones they don’t. The quality of the feed going in also plays a key role in determining the quality of what comes out.


Those constraints forced a discipline: design the signals that tell you the system is healthy, and build them before you need them. That discipline is why I could walk up to an unfamiliar unit, labeled in a language I didn’t read, and troubleshoot it. The operating principles were shared, and the technology-specific knowledge was easy to layer on top. That kind of control scales, because it doesn’t depend on one person holding everything in their head. Without granular control, chemical engineers built some of the most reliable safety-critical systems in the world.


Unlike other engineering disciplines, chemical engineers don’t hand off the design and walk away. They stay accountable for how the unit runs, long after startup. That’s the job software engineering is turning into. I call it the **Software Process Engineer** .


## What a Software Process Engineer does


The Software Process Engineer isn’t the person automation left behind. They’re the person automation made indispensable.


**They own the design.** The factory is only as good as its specs. Fundamentals like systems design and knowledge of the business domain aren’t background knowledge for this role. They’re the daily craft.


**They own the health of the system.** They watch the signals on the factory health and the guardrails on what it ships. In a refinery, yield is the percentage of the feed that comes out as sellable product. Whatever missed spec gets reprocessed. Refineries call it slop. Software factories have yields too. The share of changes that need rework isn’t found by reading every line. It shows up when a change fails the tests, health, or performance checks the Software Process Engineer designed. If a factory starts producing slop, the engineer is the first to know.


**They own outcomes in production.** Signals like pod health and queue depth tell you the equipment is running, not that the process is functioning as intended. Picture a store checkout service after a refactor of how promo codes are handled. Orders still complete and nothing throws an error, but some codes now quietly apply no discount. Every dashboard stays green while customers pay full price. Only a business signal catches it, like the share of orders with a promo code that actually got the discount. A refinery would call that conversion, and it would be on the dashboard.


Underneath all of it are the tradeoffs between throughput, yield, and efficiency that deliver the most business value, not the perfectly designed system. Getting that balance right is the heart of process engineering, but it only works if you can see the system clearly.


That’s the discipline that allowed me to walk onto unfamiliar units around the world and still optimize them. Software can work that way too, with systems you can trust without reading every line. The most valuable engineers of this next era will be the ones who build those systems and avoid the curse of granular control.
